p: Okay. So, 1,300 people for SNAP to manage almost well, 29.5 thousand uh applications monthly? Is that accurate?
Yes.
Okay and 1,700 people for 46,000, almost 47,000 cash assistance roles?
Yup.

855 for almost 29,000 a month for Medicaid and 161 plus we’ll say for well, we didn’t get that one for you for the City FHEPS,

okay. Alright, I think the uhm, caseload sounds extreme.

Uhm, it is large numbers. I will say uhm, you know the SNAP, Cash Assistance and Medicaid programs uhm, and City FHEPS, they don’t operate on a caseload basis in regards to like a worker is assigned specific cases.
Right.

Uhm, that’s how we used to work uh, when individuals had to be assigned to a specific center and that’s the only place they could receive services. Uh, when we move to a citywide uh, approach to this, uh, the way in which things work is we have systems where workers can just take the next case that is in front of them. It can be from anywhere across the city, which is a far more efficient way for us to actually process the work and make sure that we are moving through the work uh correctly but yes, it is a large -
I guess workload is maybe the word I should have used but either way, it sounds like it’s a lot of work for not that many people. Uhm, by program how many of these positions are currently filled?
Uhm, sure. For SNAP, uhm, the latest number I have is 1,093. For cash assistance, uhm, I have - you know I don’t have the headcount for cash assistance.
Okay, what about Medicaid and City FHEPS?
Uh, you know actually City FHEPS also, I only have the programmatic budget. So, we’ll get back to you on that one.
Okay and Medicaid?
And Medicaid 710.
I would also note I think our numbers are a little older so we’ll make sure - we’ll follow up with more accurate account numbers.
Okay thank you and what’s the average salary for each position?
I’ll also have to get back to you on that. We didn’t - I don’t have that with me.

Okay, uhm, is the need greater than what is budgeted? So, given the workload, you know and the number of employees that you have and the retention rate, uhm, and the

timeliness rate, do you think that the number of employees you have currently is sufficient?

Uhm, I think our uh headcount as budgeted is sufficient. I think as uh, we discussed earlier, making sure that we are keeping all of our vacancies filled is really a priority for us. Uhm, and then that will really indicate to us if there are still gaps in staffing or not. Uhm, but uh I do believe you know the budgeted headcount we’re seeing in the SNAP, cash and Medicaid program you know, we are able to you know manage the volume. There are obviously months that may be a spike that is anomaly uhm but our focus is really on making sure that we’re keeping - we’re as close to the headcount as possible and then that can inform to us if we think there might be an additional need and if so, we would then have a conversation with
Okay, that’s fair. Is HRA currently using overtime to meet the demand?

We are currently. We do utilize overtime within the programs as needed. Uhm, uh, you know we have not had to utilize mandatory overtime in a very long time except in a few specific instances that were again anomalous.
Okay, uhm, would you happen to know how many hours and what the cost is for the few occasions you’ve had to use it?
For mandatory overtime, we’d have to get back to you on that or -
Any type of overtime.
Right, I think on - we’ll get back to you on that. I’m assuming it’s in relation to those programs you’re talking about, correct?

Yes and uh, we just talked about this but I was doing just my own, I didn’t even do the math. I’m just looking at the numbers but I would love to know if you have the current case ratio for SNAP, cash assistance, Medicaid and rental assistance and how that compares to the optimal case ratio?
Sure, we can get back to you on that uhm, I think we need to talk to our folks about cash and SNAP because we don’t think about it in case ratio.
I was going to say perhaps work ratio or whatever metric you want to call it.
We can come back to you on that.

Okay great, alright moving into uh, City of Yes. The City Council secured $5 billion in commitments as part of the City for All housing plan in recognition of the importance of advancing a holistic housing plan that could support working and middle class New Yorkers and invest in solutions that meet their housing needs. Of the $5 billion dollars, 187 million was committed over ten years for City FHEPS vouchers and social services to create permanent homes for those in the DHS shelter system. This commitment included an investment of $122 million over 10 years for affordable housing service contracts. Was the funding added as a new need for affordable housing services in the Preliminary Plan part of this commitment?
Uhm, yes it was. Uhm, we did as part of the uhm Preliminary budget - hold on one second. I’m so sorry. Uhm, it looks like uh we have $215 million for the City FHEPS vouchers.
Yeah, let me make sure, hold on. I’m sorry. You know that actually is part of the original commitment, which covered Fiscal Years ‘25 and ‘26, so.
So, no it wasn’t added as a new need?
Uhm, it would have been but not in the Preliminary Budget, the previous budget.
Sorry?
It was added previously.
It was added previously - oh, affordable housing services specifically? Not overall City

Oh, I’m sorry. Uhm, yeah, I mean uh no, the affordable housing services money that was added to the budget uhm, like the rest of our cliffs was added to cover our anticipated spending for the AHS program. As per the uhm, uh previous Administrations commitment.
Okay, are you working with other city agencies on this?

Uhm, I mean, we do work with other city agencies uhm on the construction. AHS is a program that uhm, largely develops new affordable housing programs. So we would work with the normal city agencies uhm, like HPD or uhm, City Planning and Department of Building on AHS.
Okay and how many new units will be available with this funding?
Uhm, right now we have - we financed about 491 new units. Uhm, we have additional units in our pipeline.
How many additional?
Uhm, uh 226.
226, okay thanks.
Oh, I’m sorry. I’m so sorry. Uh, I gave you the wrong- I gave you last year's numbers. The current number of active units is 561 and we have an additional 226 in our pipeline.
226, okay and then how many of them are currently used by voucher holders?
Uhm, AHS is -
They all would be. AHS is uh -
100 percent?
Financed uhm, based upon City
Okay and when do you expect all of the new units to come online? Those additional 226?

Uhm, one building I believe is more imminent uhm, but I can get some clarity from my

uh development team to - to understand when those two, we should see them available and see moveouts.
Okay and what’s HRA’s process for selecting and placing City FHEPS voucher holders in those units?

Uhm, we look at it in the same way that we look at uhm, any rent above a building in regards to we will work closely with our DHS colleagues uhm to you know let them know that a new building is coming on in a certain number of units and then we will work together to uh target appropriate referrals to those buildings. Those buildings, I will say, tend to often rent up relatively quickly.

It’s crucial that the funding allocated as part of the City for All commitment is targeted to those at the highest risk. How is HRA ensuring that the most vulnerable people are reached with this funding.

SImilarly- similar process we work very closely with our colleagues at DHS depending on uh the affordable housing you know site and what specific services it may or may not offer - so because we want to make sure that we are making the

most successful permanent housing connections as possible.

Great. Okay give me just one moment please. Okay, uhm, rental assistance programs and source of income discrimination. In March 2026, a panel of five upstate judges ruled against the landmark state law that bans discrimination against people who use government assistance to pay their rent, stating that it violates the constitutional rights of property owners because the program requires building safety inspections. Has HRA evaluated the potential implications of this ruling for the city? And specifically for the City FHEPS program?
I think we are currently assessing its potential implication for the city.
Okay, it can’t be good I would state. Uhm, to date, how many source of income discrimination complaints have been filed by HRA clients attempting to use City FHEPS vouchers in Fiscal 2026?
So, source of income discrimination complaints would actually be directed to
CCHR yeah, but you don’t know how many of your clients might -
I don’t have that information here. We can look to see if we have anything but CCHR would have the official numbers.

Okay, we’ll make sure to ask them on that. Uhm, and then how does HRA work with CCHR to address source of income discrimination complaints from clients attempting to use City FHEPS vouchers? Is there anything like do you - you know make sure people know their rights, the law etc.?

Yes, we - throughout the process, we make sure uh when individuals are utilizing a subsidy that they have information on their rights. If they think that they are being discriminated against, how they can go about filing a complaint? Uhm, and then obviously if CCHR reaches out to us, we would engage with them fully to support uhm whatever they might be looking at uh that impacted our clients.

Uhm, and an ongoing concern - sorry, I’m moving to domestic violence services. An ongoing concern of both the Council and advocates for several years has been the adequacy of the city’s DV Shelter capacity to fully meet the need. Many individuals who would benefit from the specialized services available in DV facilities, end up in the DHS shelter system where such support services are not available, even though they are deemed eligible for DV Shelter. I understand that the current DV capacity includes 2,290 emergency beds and 628 units in DV Tier 2 facilities. These figures have not changed since Fiscal 2024. Does the current DV shelter system have enough capacity to meet the level of demand? And also, I would just ask and I don’t know if you have this or not but I know that uhm, the DV cases of domestic violence went up significantly during the pandemic and so, I’m wondering if those numbers now are similar to those numbers or if they’re more similar to prepandemic levels?

I do not have that data with me but we can look into it. Uhm, and you know you are correct on the number of uh domestic - DV Shelter beds that we have. I will say though that we work

closely with our DHS providers and they are required to make sure that they are connecting families who are experiencing domestic violence with appropriate services. Uhm, and uhm you know at times there are uh decisions made by families who would choose to - would prefer to actually go into the DHS system rather than come into the DV system. So, we’re constantly -
What are some of the reasons for that, do you know?

Uhm, I think that uh there are in the DV system, there are some additional sort of rules and requirements that uhm need to be complied with in the system that aren’t necessarily the same rules and requirements in the DHS system. Much of the DV system is the emergency system especially is overseen by the Office of Children and Family Services at the state. So, they really dictate to us uh, all of the real regulations and they are more of the direct oversight of those systems, even though we facilitate on our end. Uhm, much of the operations of that system are really dedicated by OCFS.
Can you share any details about additional Tier 2 units for emergency beds that might be in the pipeline?

Uhm, we don’t have anything specifically that is currently in the pipeline. Uhm, but we are constantly you know looking and assessing and discussing with our partners at OMB if more beds would be you know appropriate. I think one of the challenges in the DV system as well is for a family or an individual, a single adult, uhm, there may be multiple factors that need to be taken into account around placement. Uhm, which is why we’re very thankful to our colleagues at DHS. Uhm, you know that sort of provides additional coverage because too I think map out and try to understand within the DV system, the location size and other units that we would need across uhm is challenging, which is why the close partnership with DHS helps to ensure that we’re able to place families and individuals.
Uhm, what’s the average vacancy rate for Tier 2 units and DV emergency beds?

So, uh, the Tier 2, oh, I’m sorry, the emergency beds, has an occupancy rate of as of December, of uhm approximately 85 percent. Uhm, and

I will get back to you on the Tier 2 because I don’t seem to have that here on the sheet but we’ll get back to you.
Okay, and how is DHS working to better address the unique needs of those impacted by domestic violence who reside within the regular DHS shelter system?

Thank you for the question Chair. Uhm, as we do uhm around all needs of our clients constantly working with our city partners, including the Mayor’s Office to End Gender and Domestic Violence around best practices, training materials, engagement strategies, going out into shelters to make sure that our staff, our provider staff is comfortable having conversations around domestic violence. That they’re doing it with sensitivity and empathy. Uhm and making sure that the warm handoffs from the DV system continues so that if they’re nonresidential services that somebody is receiving, they continue to get those with us.

And we also - I’d just say also make sure that we coordinate closely HRA runs a series of nonresidential programs as well as our

colleagues at NGBV. So we have closely connected referral pathways between us as well.

Okay, thank you. Okay, going back to asylum seeker response, uhm as of February 28th this year, there were 29,809 asylum seekers in the city’s care, mostly in the DHS system. DHS will be taking over as the lead agency in the city’s response and integrating asylum seekers into its existing shelter system as we discussed. Uhm, DHS’s Preliminary Plan includes $1.15 billion in Fiscal ‘26, $1.2 billion in Fiscal ‘27 and $498.4 million in Fiscals 2028 and 2029 for asylum seeker expenses. How were these costs estimated and what services are provided with these funds and how do they address the unique needs of asylum seekers. You addressed that earlier but how are the costs estimated and what services are provided?

The uhm, special population support services funding uhm in the budget is somewhat of a legacy budget. If you recall, when other agencies were operating different shelters, all of the budget - budgeted funding was uhm placed within DHS’s budget. And then it was allocated on a periodic basis. So, uhm, the budget that we have now

is based on our best projections of how many asylees that we would serve. Uhm, but the - the dollar amount uhm and how it was set is largely done on uhm, earlier right, on earlier projections from past years.

Okay, thank you and the enhanced cost of the provision of shelter for asylum seekers during the Adam’s Administration was a result of the reliance on emergency contracts, including those for hotels that were held by agencies outside of DHS. You may know that the Speaker's Bill on Emergency Contracting, Intro. Number 2 is now on the Mayor’s desk awaiting signature. It limits emergency contracts to 90 days unless prior approval is granted by the Comptroller and requires audits 15 days after execution. If a contract is not submitted for audit within 15 days, the contract would be voided. The Council passed this bill to save the city money on expense of emergency contracts and to ensure procurement goes through the proper channels. Does DHS have any remaining emergency contracts related to asylum seekers?

We’re currently in the process of transitioning uhm, emergency contracts that will end

in June to new contracts effective July, standard shelter contracts.
Okay, so uh no additional services or programs will be contracted post July?
I can speak only to the shelters that were under contract under the emergency contracts.
Okay, thank you. Uhm, and how much do you anticipate the full integration of asylum seekers into the DHS system will impact costs?

I would defer to Chief Johns, however, our system is integrated in that as clients are coming in, they’re being placed in the shelters that are available at the services that are available. So, I’m not sure that there’s a -
I mean if the outyear projections are accurate, then it seems like there will be a cost savings but.
Uhm, yeah, I mean generally speaking, uhm, the shelters, they’re moving into the standard shelters would be cheaper.

Uhm, okay this might be a little redundant but will there be any cost savings

realized by this integration given that DHS already has experienced in the provision of shelter?

Uhm, no, I mean we are not projecting cost savings as it relates to that. I mean, if you look at the budget historically, you would have seen adjustments made to the budget related to the uhm, the change in the population but uhm, not related to the integration.

Okay, thank you. Uhm, okay and then just uh some follow up to Council Member Nurses questions earlier. Uhm on February 19th, Gothamist reported that the Administration would restart homeless encampment sweeps, which had been paused earlier in the year. Given that the Mayor had been critical of sweeps conducted under the de Blasio and in Adams Administrations, this was a bit surprising. The Administration has stated that DHS will be the main responding agency for future sweeps, whereas NYPD was the primary responding agency in prior sweeps. Can you share more about what this would look like and how it would be different from past sweep operations?

Sure, I’m happy to start here. Uhm, and as I said, I think the move to have the Department of Homeless Services to take the lead makes good sense. And I personally don’t think of these as cleanings or sweeps or moves but as focused housing efforts. We focus our housing efforts on all different parts of the population, whether it’s at the end of the subway line or I’ve heard about you know the top 50 list of people we’re really focused on who have really entrenched needs. Why not focus on people who are staying in a specific place and make sure that they have focused outreach and support around housing and next steps. So, yes, I think DHS is the right lead. These are the outreach workers who have built the relationships. We know where the spaces are. Then we can also hear first hand what people need and want and make sure that those offerings are available as we do our planning for the future. Uhm, making sure that peoples uh - peoples stuff, uh, is cared for, understanding their family situation and making sure they’re placed in the best possible environment.

Okay, thank you. And uhm, what if the sweeps encounter a homeless individual in

the encampments who doesn’t want to enter shelter? How will that be handled?

Yeah and I haven’t even had a chance to sit in with the teams yet to understand what they do. So, I don’t want to answer there but I think you know we do want to be pursuing relentless engagement and we certainly cannot force people to take shelter options.
I would say that’s a good answer.
Okay.

Uhm, alright, how will - how will folks who are encountered, be connected to services in shelters? So, I know you’re not deep into this yet but my understanding is that you have some experience in this area, so maybe we can speak a little aspirationally about what should happen and what the best -

Yeah, I would love to. Uhm, I think it is actually important to set kind of non-negotiables for the way we engage with people. I did want to know in my previous job and want to know here, uhm, the by name list of people that we’re engaging. Uhm, their housing preferences, we had a

specific housing preference form to understand what people preferred and other social services they needed. I want to know what we offer to people and I want to know what we offer to people. Uhm and I want to know what they will do given that the place that they’ve been staying will no longer be a place that they can stay in the future. And I think uhm, in my experience, which may vary as I come here, uhm most people, if offered the things that they really need, will take those offers. Uhm, and be stably housed at least for some period where we can start to provide other social services.
Okay, uhm, a common criticism of sweeps in the past has been that many unsheltered peoples belongings were thrown away. How will you ensure that this doesn’t happen?

And I will be happy to let the Administrator speak about this as well but I think that uhm, you know that that kind of practice should not be allowed. We should understand what people have with them, what they will be able to take with them and what they want to take with them and make sure that that uhm, those materials get inventoried and that they can retrieve them. And then anything

that is left, we mark as left, right? I think it’s also really important to our partners who do the actual cleanups to make sure that we haven’t left something behind that people want right. We have to leave that space clear for them to do their proper work. So, I think the issue of people's belongings is a really important one.

Okay and uhm you know I know again you’re still just getting your feet under you but in past cases we’ve seen you know Department of Sanitation, that’s usually engaged in these types of sweeps. Literally throwing peoples belongings right in front of them into the back of the sanitation trucks. Uhm, items for their children. Uhm, you know and obviously just valuable items to them uhm deemed invaluable by you know city employees. So, just flagging that for your awareness. Did you want to add anything Administrator?

Thank you Chair. I would just add as the Commissioner mentioned, especially for those who have accepted placement, making sure that we are working with them to bring in items within limit, things that are important to them but

also ensuring that we’re maintaining the health and safety of all of our clients.
Understood. Do you have lockers or storage for sweeps?
Yes, there uhm is storage that DHS manages, so we will kind of inventory with the individual what they are not going to take with them and we will store that for them.
And I assume that’s free of cost?
It is free of cost.

Okay, thank you. And uhm, again you may not have this direct information right now but how will DH- but you might actually. So, how will DHS identify encampment sites for sweeps? Like do you have already a list of locations identified?
We do and we work with our partner agencies, elected officials, uhm, community members to identify and assess areas of concern. So, this is an ongoing uhm practice.

Okay, thank you. Okay, alright, I think we’re getting into the home stretch here. Uhm, capital plan budgeting. In the recently released Preliminary Capital Commitment Plan for

Fiscals 2026 - 2030, both HRA and DHS had virtually no changes in funding since the adopted capital plan. No funding was adjusted for any of the major HRA capital projects, such as computer equipment and technology upgrades, improvements to HRA facilities or communication systems. In DHS, no funding was added for the single room shelter units in upper Manhattan that the Administration announced in February the Bellevue Men’s Shelter and intake facility, which will be closing this month for repairs, also did not receive any additional funding, nor did the East 3rd Street and Bowery Shelter sites, which will become intake centers following Bellevue’s closure and may require capital funding to accommodate more clients. Why were there no adjustments to the capital budgets for HRA and DHS?

Uhm, yes, thank you for that question. Uhm, so part - so there are a number of initiatives that you had noted. Some of them uhm, we didn’t have the estimates prior to the Capital Plan locking. Uhm, but for the most part, we’ve worked really closely with the - our partners at the Office of Management and Budget particularly through uhm,

uhm, the last you know number of months to align our capital budget. So, while we didn’t add money, we are moving money around to ensure that we have funds in the places that we think we’ll need it. Uhm and we also have uhm, money in lines where we can move it and make it available uhm, but at the time of the capital budget, we did not have uhm, a need to make a request for additional funds.
Okay. That sounds like uhm, a bit of a budget dance there. You’re saying you’re just going to move funds for certain projects to other projects?

Uhm, no what I think what I’m saying is that there are some needs like uhm, uhm, Bellevue, which we didn’t know at the time of that- the budget lock. So, there will have to be adjustments made for that but there are some needs that we are aware of. We’ve been uhm at some of our sites that -
That you’re saying you have the funding for, okay, alright.
Yeah.

For example, and at the risk of adding an example where I could be wrong but uhm

being at 83rd a few times now, uhm, I believe for example that there’s an elevator upgrade that has already been budgeted as part of the normal capital planning uhm for the existing site.
Okay, got it, okay thank you. Uhm, so and I guess this goes back to your earlier statement, has capital needs assessment been conducted since adoption?
Uhm, that’s a good question. Uh, I’ll have to get back to you, that’s not in my area but uhm, we’ll get back to you on that.
Okay and how often are capital needs assessments required?
Uhm, again, yeah, I’m sorry, I’m just not aware of that. I mean we will get the information to you.
Okay. Uhm, okay then you might have the answer to this one. Has an assessment been made of what repairs are necessary at Bellevue and what the capital cost may be?
I don’t think there’s been an assessment of that done at this time.

Okay. Alrighty we’ll follow up on all of those. Okay, alright, thanks, okay. Uhm, okay more City FHEPS. Uh, City FHEPS has grown exponentially since the inception of the program in 2018. The initial budget for City FHEPS was only $26.3 million growing to $1.78 billion in Fiscal 2026 as of the Preliminary Plan and growing to a projected budget of $3.04 billion by Fiscal 2029. As the program is approaching the one decade mark, we would like to discuss key takeaways and what the future of City FHEPS could look like. Can HRA detail what has worked effectively within the City FHEPS program? What has not worked? And what lessons have been learned since its inception?

I think we’re very happy to set up a separate time to sort of go more in depth there on that but I think the- you know I think the program has been very successful in moving people out, right, connecting people to permanent housing. Uhm, I think you know it’s very clear that the program has effectively done that. I think as the Commissioner said, right, we do need to look at you know ongoing of the program right from a sustainability point of view. Uhm, but I think that

you know it has proven itself to be a respected tool within the community and connecting with landlords. So, uhm that I think you know is proven in the 66,000 or 68,000 households currently utilizing the program. Uh, there are obviously things we’re going to be looking at in regards to ongoing you know management of the program and how can we make sure we’re effectively connecting people to services that also offer a offramp from the program because we’ve connected people to good paying jobs and employment that allows them self sustainability and those are I think some of the- some of the key things but we are happy to set up time to discuss at further detail.
Okay, that sounds good. I look forward to it but uhm just to clarify some of the workforce programs, it sounds like are improvements that you might want to make in terms of -

Uh, yeah, some of the - the City FHEPS specific targeted programs that we had discussed before. We hadn’t had just one that was specifically focused on City FHEPS. So, that is I think one of the things we would be looking at to connect more individuals to services that can support

them in, you know the progression of an individual's career.
Okay, sounds good. What is the number of City FHEPS voucher holders who lost their housing and subsequently returned to shelter within one year in each of the Fiscal’s 2024, 2025, and 2026 to date.
We’ll have to get back to you with that data.
Okay. And also, I’d like to know how many return to shelter within two years. So, within one year and within two years.
